panels.title: Health
panels.description:
NAME
    Health — aggregate pool state

DESCRIPTION
    The single-value state ZFS assigns to the pool. ZFS classifies a
    pool as one of: ONLINE, DEGRADED, FAULTED, OFFLINE, REMOVED, or
    UNAVAIL. The state is the same value `zpool status` reports.

EQUIVALENT IN OTHER TOOLS
    In a non-ZFS Linux storage stack there is no single equivalent.
    The same information is distributed across:
        mdadm --detail            array layout, member state, sync
                                  progress (software RAID only).
        lvs / vgs / pvs           volume manager state.
        cryptsetup status         per-mapping encryption state.
        dmsetup status            device-mapper target state.
        fsck output / dmesg       filesystem-detected errors.
    None of those tools reports block-level checksum errors, because
    none of those layers performs end-to-end checksumming. A silent
    data corruption (bit rot, controller bug, cable error) that
    bypasses RAID parity is invisible to that stack until an
    application reads the data and notices it is wrong.

    ZFS combines volume management, redundancy, encryption, and
    end-to-end checksums into one subsystem with one reported state.

SOURCE
    zfs_exporter polls `zpool list -H -o name,health` every scrape
    interval (15s default) and emits:
        zfs_pool_health{pool="..."}
    Numeric values map to:
        0   ONLINE
        1   DEGRADED
        2   FAULTED
        3   OFFLINE
        4   REMOVED
        5   UNAVAIL

FIELDS
    ONLINE      Normal operation. All vdevs reachable and healthy.
    DEGRADED    A vdev failure has occurred but redundancy is
                tolerating it. Service continues. Investigate which
                vdev (zpool status) and replace before redundancy is
                exhausted.
    FAULTED     The pool cannot be opened in its current state.
                Service is down for any dataset on this pool.
    OFFLINE     Operator explicitly took a vdev offline.
    REMOVED     A vdev was physically removed at runtime.
    UNAVAIL     A vdev is missing on import (disk gone, path moved).

CAVEATS
    This panel reports the pool's overall state only. Per-vdev
    detail, specific error counts, and recovery progress are not
    here. Use the zed events panel (#12) for individual vdev
    transitions and zpool status(8) for full per-vdev state.

SEE ALSO
    Panel #12 — zed events. Live transitions of vdev state.
    zpool(8) status — full pool state as a tree.
    /etc/zfs/zpool.cache — last-known layout.
    Documentation/admin-guide/zfs-tuning.rst — Linux kernel notes.

panels.title: ARC Hit Rate
panels.description:
NAME
    ARC Hit Rate — read requests served from the in-kernel cache

DESCRIPTION
    Percentage of read requests served from the ZFS Adaptive
    Replacement Cache (ARC) without reaching the underlying vdevs,
    computed over a 5-minute rolling window.

EQUIVALENT IN OTHER TOOLS
    The Linux page cache, used by ext4/xfs/btrfs, does not expose an
    equivalent hit-rate metric by default. The closest approximation
    in a non-ZFS stack is /usr/share/bcc/tools/cachestat — an eBPF
    tool that traces page-cache events in real time. Two structural
    differences make the numbers not directly comparable:

        Eviction policy. The Linux page cache is LRU (Least Recently
        Used). ARC is MRU+MFU (Most Recently Used + Most Frequently
        Used, with a ghost list to detect repeated misses). For
        repeated random-access workloads — database working sets,
        for example — ARC retains hot data through scans that would
        evict the page cache.

        Scope. The page cache covers all filesystems' read I/O. ARC
        covers ZFS read I/O specifically. The two can coexist; ZFS
        sets primarycache=metadata on datasets where the application
        has its own cache (Postgres shared_buffers) to avoid
        double-caching.

    No Splunk, Loki, or Dynatrace panel reports ARC hit rate by
    default. Some Splunk apps include cachestat output if it was
    scraped to a log file, in which case the data is sampled and
    delayed, not real-time.

SOURCE
    zfs_exporter reads /proc/spl/kstat/zfs/arcstats every scrape
    interval (15s default) and exposes per-counter gauges:
        zfs_arcstat{metric="hits"}
        zfs_arcstat{metric="misses"}
    Query:
        100 * rate(hits[5m]) / rate(hits+misses[5m])

FIELDS
    > 95 %     Working set fits comfortably in ARC.
    80 - 95 %  Healthy with occasional capacity misses.
    < 80 %     Working set exceeds ARC capacity. Consider larger
               primarycache, more system RAM allocated to ZFS, or
               L2ARC if read pattern justifies it.
    Sudden drops to near-0 % indicate either a cache flush (e.g.,
    primarycache property change on a busy dataset) or a large new
    dataset displacing the working set.

CAVEATS
    Hit rate is system-wide, not per-dataset. A high overall rate
    can mask a poor rate on one specific dataset. The arcstats
    counters are accumulative from boot; if the ZFS module is
    reloaded, the rate calculation resets.

SEE ALSO
    Panel #8 — ARC Size vs Target. Shows current cache size and
        how it compares to the configured target.
    /proc/spl/kstat/zfs/arcstats — raw counters.
    /usr/share/bcc/tools/cachestat — page cache equivalent.
    zfs(8) primarycache property documentation.
    Sun Solaris ARC paper (Megiddo & Modha, 2003) — original design.
